strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: adversarial robustness of DL-based MRI reconstruction
Sound mathematical foundation with formal analysis (Theorem 1) of attack propagation in k-space
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, network architectures, and attack types

Well-organized presentation with extensive implementation details in appendices
Realistic threat model including unsupervised attacks and herringbone artifacts
weaknesses: Misleading core claim: Described as 'training-free' but requires expensive iterative optimization at test time for every input—this fundamentally undermines the main value proposition

Critical omission: No computational cost analysis or timing comparisons provided—Algorithm 1 requires gradient computations and multiple iterations, likely prohibitive for clinical use with MRI requiring rapid turnaround
Incomplete theoretical justification: While Theorem 1 characterizes attack propagation, the jump from theory to the proposed objective (Eq. 10) lacks rigorous justification
Limited novelty: Cyclic measurement consistency for MRI reconstruction is not new (Zhang et al. 2024, Kim et al. 2023); application to adversarial robustness is relatively straightforward
Adaptive attack evaluation limitations: Only one adaptive attack formulation tested; whether it represents true worst-case is unclear; convergence analysis missing
Missing practical considerations: No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for ε and σ, no guidance for practitioners on setting these values, no discussion of convergence conditions
No reproducibility data: No code availability, no timing information, no analysis of failure modes, unclear dataset-specific tuning procedures

strengths: Novel and creative approach: Using cyclic measurement consistency for training-free adversarial defense in MRI reconstruction is original, addressing the practical limitation that adversarial robustness training is computationally expensive

Rigorous theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 with detailed proof in Appendix G provides formal justification for why cyclic consistency detects attacks through k-space discrepancies, grounded in MRI physics

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests across 5 different DL architectures, 2 anatomies, multiple attack types/strengths, realistic scenarios (herringbone artifacts), blind setups, and adaptive adversaries—demonstrating broad applicability and honest assessment of limitations

Strong empirical results: Substantial improvements in mitigation (e.g., Cor-PD PSNR: 28.22→35.19) while maintaining clean data quality, outperforming existing defenses including adversarial training and SMUG
Practical significance: Addresses important clinical problem (adversarial robustness of DL-MRI reconstruction) with solution that doesn't require expensive retraining, reducing deployment barriers

Physics-informed design: The approach leverages MRI acquisition physics (forward operator, k-space measurement consistency) rather than purely data-driven methods, making it interpretable and domain-appropriate
Thorough documentation: Implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and comparison methods clearly described; appendices provide extensive supplementary results
weaknesses: Loose theoretical bounds: Theorem 1's error bound (Eq. 9) depends on multiple unquantified constants (singular values, coil sensitivity profiles, Laplacian constants); tightness of bounds and practical relevance unclear

Misleading 'training-free' terminology: Method requires dataset and network-dependent hyperparameter tuning (ε, σ with linear schedulers, Appendix F), conflating with truly hyperparameter-free approaches
Adaptive attack vulnerability: Under adaptive attacks aware of defense strategy, effectiveness degrades (Table 2)—method is more robust than alternatives but not fully adversarially robust
Limited theoretical characterization: Assumptions about when cyclic consistency holds (well-trained networks, specific architectures) not fully formalized; failure modes not comprehensively analyzed
Domain specialization: Approach specialized to MRI reconstruction; limited demonstration of applicability to other imaging modalities or domains
Incomplete computational analysis: Iterative Algorithm 1 requires multiple network forward/backward passes; computational cost and deployment time not quantified relative to baseline inference
Limited anatomical diversity: Evaluation on only 2 anatomical regions (knee, brain) from single dataset (fastMRI); generalization to other anatomies/protocols not demonstrated
Indirect detection mechanism: Connection between detecting k-space complement set errors (Ω^C) and successful attack mitigation is indirect; doesn't guarantee attack is fully reversed

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: adversarial robustness in medical imaging MRI reconstruction without requiring retraining
Novel training-free approach using cyclic measurement consistency that generalizes across 5 different PD-DL architectures without modification
Comprehensive experimental validation across 2 datasets, multiple attack types (PGD, FGSM, ℓ₂), and realistic scenarios including blind mitigation (unknown attack parameters)
Physically grounded approach leveraging k-space structure and MRI acquisition properties, with Theorem 3.1 providing theoretical characterization
Extensive ablation studies examining design choices, non-uniform undersampling, adaptive attacks, and herringbone artifacts
Complementary to existing defenses—can be combined with SMUG and AT for further improvements
Clear presentation of methodology with detailed implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Theorem 3.1 provides limited practical utility: the bound depends on unknown constants (Lipschitz properties) and is too loose to predict when the method will work in practice; logical connection between theoretical attack characterization and proposed cyclic consistency solution is incomplete

Prohibitive inference computational cost (6-21.3 minutes per image, 66.5 GB memory for dynamic MRI) undermines the practical advantage over training-based methods for clinical deployment where time-to-diagnosis is critical
Limited threat model—method only effective for small perturbations (ε ≤ 0.01); performance degrades significantly for larger attacks, which are realistic when adversaries are unconstrained
Limited algorithmic novelty: Algorithm 1 composes existing techniques (reverse optimization, cyclic consistency from prior work); individual components are well-known

Gaps in reproducibility: no explicit code release statement, missing experimental details (blind mitigation sampling strategy, adaptive attack information access), error bars absent from main results tables, random seeds not reported
Incomplete evaluation of defenses: limited comparison to other training-free mitigation approaches; adaptive attack evaluation (Section 4.2) could be more sophisticated

Theory-practice gap: characterization of when/why the method works relies primarily on empirical validation rather than rigorous theoretical analysis; convergence guarantees and failure mode characterization lacking

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of adversarial robustness in MRI reconstruction with clear clinical relevance
Provides theoretical grounding through Theorem 3.1 with complete proofs establishing error bounds under perturbation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple datasets (Cor-PD, Ax-FLAIR), attack types, network architectures, and realistic scenarios including blind and adaptive setups
Training-free approach is computationally efficient and practical compared to adversarial training methods
Extensive supplementary material with implementation details, ablation studies, and additional experiments enhances reproducibility
Successfully demonstrates effectiveness across different attack strengths and perturbation types without degrading clean image quality
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core technique (cyclic measurement consistency) is well-established in prior MRI work; application to adversarial defense is incremental

Weak theoretical justification: Theorem 3.1 characterizes general error propagation under perturbation but doesn't explain why adversarial attacks specifically violate cyclic consistency compared to random noise
Potential circular reasoning and security gap: detection mechanism checks cyclic consistency while the entire defense enforces it; no analysis of attacks specifically designed to maintain consistency
Modest empirical improvements: Table 1 shows marginal gains (PSNR 35.14 vs 35.14 for AT on Cor-PD) with no statistical significance testing
Highly specialized scope: limited to MRI with k-space measurements; unclear generalization to other imaging modalities or inverse problems
Questionable practical applicability: requires synthesis of k-space measurements and knowledge of forward operator, which may not reflect realistic single-acquisition MRI pipelines
Unfair experimental comparisons: AT and SMUG baselines trained on specific attack strengths naturally perform worse on different attacks; missing comparisons with physics-informed defenses
Computational efficiency claims not clearly supported: Table 3 shows higher inference time and memory consumption; additional iterations and projection operations required
Incomplete adaptive attack analysis: attacks don't specifically target the cyclic consistency check; attacker model remains somewhat artificial
Presentation density and clarity issues: key connection between cyclic consistency and adversarial robustness not explained intuitively; critical details relegated to appendices

strengths: Novel training-free defense leveraging physics-based cyclic measurement consistency, addressing the important problem of adversarial robustness in medical imaging without requiring network retraining

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Cor-PD, Ax-FLAIR), architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet), attack types (ℓ∞, ℓ2, herringbone, adaptive), and scenarios (blind, non-uniform undersampling)
Theoretical analysis with Theorem 3.1 providing formal error bounds, complete proofs in appendices, and rigorous verification of gradient obfuscation avoidance
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details (Appendices A.1-A.2), clear algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, and honest discussion of limitations and assumptions

Demonstrates effectiveness across diverse settings including blind mitigation, adaptive attacks, comparison to multiple training-free baselines (JPEG, TV, randomized smoothing, diffusion purification), and extension to other inverse problems
weaknesses: Severe computational cost: inference time ~6.78 minutes (proposed) vs 0.04-0.63 minutes for alternatives (~100-170x slowdown), severely limiting clinical deployment where speed is critical, with no practical solutions proposed
Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 3.1 uses standard unrolled network error propagation analysis; bounds depend on σ_max/σ_min but tightness unclear and utility for system design questionable

Method relies on cyclic consistency assumption that could potentially be circumvented by sophisticated adaptive attacks designed specifically to preserve cyclic consistency; assumption robustness not thoroughly analyzed
Hyperparameter sensitivity: multiple parameters (ε, iterations, δ, λ) require tuning based on attack type/strength (Table 12), undermining 'training-free' claim for truly blind scenarios

Scalability concerns: memory consumption increases dramatically with dimensionality (Table 3: 30.5GB for 2D dynamic to 66.5GB for 3D dynamic); limited evaluation on 3D MRI; mixed results on applicability to other inverse problems (Sections M-N)
